alignments.english: But we have seen that power itself rests on something other than force, on narratives, on consent, on belief in its legitimacy.

alignments.french: La force seule ne fait pas tenir une société ; elle peut contraindre un temps, mais une société qui ne tiendrait que par la contrainte serait précaire, sans cesse menacée, incapable de la coopération spontanée sans laquelle la vie commune se défait.
alignments.english: Force alone does not hold a society together; it can constrain for a time, but a society that would only hold together through constraint would be precarious, constantly threatened, incapable of the spontaneous cooperation without which communal life falls apart.

alignments.french: La force explique peut-être qu'on ne se révolte pas ; elle n'explique pas qu'on coopère, qu'on se fasse confiance, qu'on tienne ensemble.
alignments.english: Force may explain why there is no revolt; it does not explain why we cooperate, why we trust each other, why we hold together.

alignments.french: On pourrait alors invoquer l'intérêt : une société tiendrait parce que chacun y trouve son compte, parce que la coopération est avantageuse, parce qu'il est rationnel de vivre ensemble plutôt que seul.
alignments.english: One could then invoke interest: a society holds together because everyone finds their benefit in it, because cooperation is advantageous, because it is rational to live together rather than alone.

alignments.french: Cette explication, plus profonde que celle de la force, saisit une part de vérité : les sociétés reposent bien, pour une part, sur l'intérêt mutuel, sur les avantages de la coopération.
alignments.english: This explanation, deeper than that of force, captures a part of the truth: societies do indeed rest, in part, on mutual interest, on the advantages of cooperation.

alignments.french: Car l'intérêt seul ne fonde pas la confiance sans laquelle la coopération est impossible ; il n'explique pas pourquoi les individus respectent leurs engagements même quand il serait avantageux de les trahir, pourquoi ils se font confiance, pourquoi ils placent parfois le bien commun au-dessus de leur intérêt.
alignments.english: For interest alone does not establish the trust without which cooperation is impossible; it does not explain why individuals respect their commitments even when it would be advantageous to betray them, why they trust each other, why they sometimes place the common good above their own interest.

alignments.french: Une société de purs calculateurs, chacun ne cherchant que son avantage, se déferait, car nul ne pourrait se fier à personne.
alignments.english: A society of pure calculators, each seeking only their own advantage, would fall apart, for no one could trust anyone.

alignments.french: L'intérêt suppose, pour fonctionner, une confiance qu'il ne suffit pas à produire.
alignments.english: Interest presupposes, to function, a trust that it does not suffice to produce.

alignments.french: Qu'est-ce donc qui tient une société, par-delà la force et l'intérêt ?
alignments.english: So what holds a society together, beyond force and interest?

alignments.french: Des liens plus invisibles, plus profonds, que l'on peine à nommer mais dont on mesure l'importance quand ils viennent à manquer.
alignments.english: Invisible links, deeper ones, that are hard to name but whose importance we measure when they are lacking.

alignments.french: Il y a la confiance, ce lien fragile qui fait qu'on peut compter les uns sur les autres, sans lequel ni l'échange, ni la coopération, ni la vie commune ne sont possibles ; une société où la confiance s'effondre se défait, quels que soient la force qui la contraint et l'intérêt qui la lie.
alignments.english: There is trust, this fragile link that allows us to count on each other, without which neither exchange, nor cooperation, nor communal life is possible; a society where trust collapses falls apart, regardless of the force that constrains it and the interest that binds it.

alignments.french: Il y a les valeurs partagées, ces représentations communes de ce qui est juste, bien, désirable, qui donnent aux individus un monde commun, un langage, des repères.
alignments.english: There are shared values, these common representations of what is just, good, desirable, which give individuals a common world, a language, reference points.

alignments.french: Il y a le sacré, ce que nous avons évoqué, ces choses tenues pour intangibles, ces absolus partagés qui fondent l'appartenance à une même communauté.
alignments.english: There is the sacred, what we have mentioned, those things held to be intangible, those shared absolutes that found belonging to the same community.

alignments.french: Il y a le récit commun, l'histoire qu'une société se raconte sur elle-même, qui relie ses membres en un même « nous ».
alignments.english: There is the common narrative, the story that a society tells about itself, which connects its members in a shared 'us'.

alignments.french: Ces liens invisibles ont ceci de commun qu'ils relèvent non de la contrainte ni du calcul, mais de la croyance, du sentiment, de l'appartenance.
alignments.english: These invisible links have in common that they arise not from constraint or calculation, but from belief, feeling, belonging.

alignments.french: Ils ne se décrètent pas, ne s'imposent pas par la force, ne se réduisent pas à l'intérêt ; ils se tissent lentement, se transmettent, s'entretiennent, et se défont quand on cesse d'en prendre soin.
alignments.english: They are not decreed, they are not imposed by force, they are not reduced to interest; they are woven slowly, transmitted, maintained, and undone when we cease to care for them.

alignments.french: Une société tient par ces liens fragiles autant que par ses institutions visibles ; et quand ils se délitent — quand la confiance s'effondre, quand les valeurs communes se dissolvent, quand plus rien n'est tenu pour sacré, quand le récit commun se défait —, aucune force ni aucun intérêt ne suffit à maintenir ensemble ce qui n'est plus relié.
alignments.english: A society holds together by these fragile links as much as by its visible institutions; and when they fray — when trust collapses, when shared values dissolve, when nothing is held sacred anymore, when the common narrative falls apart — no force or interest is enough to keep together what is no longer connected.

alignments.french: Les sociétés ne meurent pas seulement de leurs conflits visibles ; elles meurent aussi, plus silencieusement, de l'effritement des liens invisibles qui les tenaient.
alignments.english: Societies do not only die from their visible conflicts; they also die, more silently, from the erosion of the invisible links that held them.

alignments.french: Comprendre ce qui tient une société, c'est donc reconnaître l'importance de ces liens que la modernité, éprise de force et d'intérêt, tend à négliger.
alignments.english: Understanding what holds a society together is thus to recognize the importance of these links that modernity, enamored with force and interest, tends to neglect.

alignments.french: C'est comprendre que la confiance, les valeurs partagées, le sacré, le récit commun, ne sont pas des survivances archaïques dont une société rationnelle pourrait se passer, mais les conditions mêmes de la vie commune, ce sans quoi ni la force ni l'intérêt ne suffisent à faire tenir les hommes ensemble.
alignments.english: It is to understand that trust, shared values, the sacred, the common narrative, are not archaic survivals that a rational society could do without, but the very conditions of communal life, without which neither force nor interest is sufficient to keep people together.

alignments.french: Et c'est mesurer la fragilité de ces liens, la nécessité d'en prendre soin, le péril de les laisser se déliter.
alignments.english: And it is to measure the fragility of these links, the necessity of caring for them, the peril of allowing them to erode.

alignments.french: Une société n'est jamais assurée de durer ; elle repose sur des liens invisibles qu'il faut sans cesse entretenir, et dont l'effritement, plus que toute menace extérieure, la met en péril.
alignments.english: A society is never guaranteed to last; it rests on invisible links that must be constantly maintained, and whose erosion, more than any external threat, puts it at risk.

alignments.french: Prendre soin de ce qui nous relie — la confiance, les valeurs, le sens du commun — est peut-être la tâche la plus essentielle, et la plus négligée, de toute vie en société.
alignments.english: Caring for what connects us — trust, values, a sense of the common good — is perhaps the most essential, and the most neglected, task of all social life.

sentences: I had a toothache for two weeks.
At first, it was a small pain, only when I drank something cold.
I knew I had to go to the dentist.
But I don't like the dentist.
So I waited.
I took pain medication and avoided cold drinks.
After ten days, the pain got stronger.
One night, I couldn't sleep at all.
The next morning, I called.
The secretary offered me an appointment three weeks later.
"Three weeks?"
"But it hurts a lot!"
"There is a cancellation tomorrow at eight o'clock.
Does that work for you?"
I said yes immediately.
In the waiting room, I was as nervous as a child.
The dentist looked at my tooth for two minutes, then he took an X-ray.
"You have a fairly deep cavity.
If you had come earlier, it would have been simple.
Now, it's a bit more work, but it is still repairable."
He gave me an injection, then he worked for forty minutes.
It wasn't pleasant, but I hardly felt anything.
As I was leaving, he told me a phrase that I haven't forgotten: "A tooth that hurts never heals on its own."
Since then, I go twice a year.
We often conceive of morality as a set of rules: do not lie, do not steal, do not harm, keep your promises.
To be moral, in this view, would mean knowing these rules and following them; the moral person would be one who obeys the rules, while the immoral person would be one who transgresses them.
This conception has its strengths and conveniences: it provides clear guidelines, specific prohibitions, and an apparently simple criterion for right conduct.
But it may be insufficient, and we must ask whether morality really reduces to rules, or if it requires something that rules cannot capture.
Let us first acknowledge what rules have that is useful and necessary.

They provide stable reference points, valid for everyone, independent of circumstances and individuals; they protect against arbitrariness, against the rationalizations through which one justifies their faults, and against the weakness that yields to temptations.
A morality without rules, which would decide everything on a case-by-case basis according to circumstances, would risk arbitrariness, complacency, and uncertainty.
Moral rules have the virtue of establishing firm limits, prohibitions that are non-negotiable, a foundation upon which conduct can rely.
It would be naive to want a morality without any rules.
But rules also have their limits, as moral experience reveals.

First, they cannot foresee all cases; life presents situations that no rule had anticipated, cases where rules contradict each other, where applying one means violating another, and where following the rule to the letter would produce an injustice.
Should the rule 'do not lie' be followed when lying would save a life threatened by a criminal?
Difficult cases, where rules are insufficient and judgment is necessary, reveal that morality cannot be reduced to the mechanical application of rules.
Beyond rules, there needs to be a judgment that knows how to apply them, weigh them, and sometimes exceed them.
Furthermore, and more profoundly, following rules is not enough to be moral in the fullest sense.
One can respect all rules out of calculation, fear, or conformity, without any real virtue; one can refrain from lying, stealing, or harming only out of fear of consequences, without any goodness.
In contrast, true morality seems to demand more than mere adherence to rules: an inner disposition, a goodness, an attention to others, a generosity that exceeds what any rule prescribes.
The rule states what should not be done; it does not articulate positive goodness, generosity, or love for one's neighbor, which are nonetheless at the heart of moral life.
One can follow all the rules and still remain a mediocre being; one can, by sometimes transgressing the letter of a rule, demonstrate a higher goodness.
That is why a long moral tradition has emphasized not rules, but virtues, character, and inner disposition.
What matters, from this perspective, is not so much following rules as being a certain kind of person: just, good, courageous, generous, capable of discernment.
Virtue is not obedience to rules, but an acquired disposition, a way of being that inclines toward good, a character shaped by habit and education.
The virtuous person does good not because a rule commands it, but because they are so disposed; they do good with precision, in concrete situations, through a discernment that no rule can replace.
The morality of virtues shifts the focus from rules to character, from obedience to being.
The truth may lie in the complementarity of these approaches.

Rules are necessary, as reference points, as safeguards, as a foundation; but they are not sufficient, as they cannot foresee everything, nor can they replace positive goodness, nor the judgment that applies them.

Morality requires both rules and the discernment that knows how to apply them, prohibitions and the virtue that transcends them toward positive good, obedience to rules and the inner disposition that alone makes one truly moral.
Reducing morality to rules is to mutilate it, forgetting its heart, which is a certain quality of the soul; but rejecting all rules in the name of virtue alone opens the door to arbitrariness.
Moral wisdom holds both: to follow just rules, but with the discernment and goodness that exceed them — for being moral is not just about obeying, but about becoming a certain kind of being.

sentences: It's the first day of school.
After two months of vacation, school starts again.
Last night, I packed my bag.
New notebooks, pens.
Everything is clean and new.
This morning, I wake up early.
I have a bit of a stomachache.
My mom is making breakfast.
"Are you nervous?" she asks.
"No," I reply.
But that's not true.
I'm putting on my new shoes.
They hurt a little.
At eight o'clock, I arrive at school.
There are a lot of students in the courtyard.
I'm looking for my friends.
Where are they?
Finally, I see Yanis!
He is taller than before.
Hi!
What class are you in?
We are looking at the lists on the wall.
I'm looking for my name...
Class 3B.
And Yanis?
He smiles.
We're together!"
The bell rings.
We enter the classroom.
A new year begins.

sentences: I arrived in this city five years ago, in September.
I remember that day very well.
I was twenty-four years old and I didn't know anyone here.
I had found a job.
So I moved in alone, with two suitcases and a few boxes.
My new apartment was completely empty.
There were no curtains, no furniture, nothing.
The floor was cold and the apartment smelled of paint.
I sat on the floor and thought, 'What am I doing here?'
In the afternoon, I went out to buy some food.
But I didn't know the neighborhood and I got lost.
I took the bus the wrong way!
I ended up at the other end of the city.
When I got home, it was eight o'clock in the evening.
I was hungry and I was tired.
Then someone knocked on the door.
It was my neighbor, a lady in her sixties.
Good evening!
I saw that you were new.
Have you eaten?
I said no.
So she invited me to dinner at her place.
We had soup and talked for two hours.
Five years later, this lady is still my neighbor.
We still have dinner together once a month.

sentences: Last year, my friend Karim asked me to lend him three hundred euros.
His car was broken down and he needed an urgent repair to get to work.
I hesitated.
Not because I didn't trust him, but because I had heard a lot of stories: friends who argue over money, families that no longer speak to each other.
Lending money is never just about money.
It's also about relationships.
In the end, I said yes.
But we did something important: we talked clearly beforehand.
We decided together: three hundred euros, to be repaid in three installments of one hundred euros each month.
Karim even wrote it in a message.
Some people find it cold between friends.
I think the opposite.
The discomfort always comes from the uncertainty: when no one knows when or how the money will be paid back.
Karim paid me back the first two months without any problem.
In the third month, he sent me a message: 'Can I pay you back the hundred euros in two weeks?
I had a bill.'
He had warned me, so it wasn't a problem.
He paid me back everything in four months instead of three.
Today, we are still friends.
And I believe we have remained friends precisely because we dared to talk about money at the beginning.

sentences: We like to believe that evil, great evil, the kind associated with atrocities and mass crimes, is the work of monsters, of exceptionally cruel beings, radically different from us.
This belief is reassuring: it places a clear boundary between evil and us, it makes criminals a separate species, it protects us from the unsettling thought that we too could be capable of such acts.
But this reassuring belief may be false, and one of the most disturbing lessons of recent history is that great evil is often committed not by monsters, but by ordinary men.
This truth, difficult to accept, deserves to be confronted, as it sheds harsh light on the fragility of civilization and our own.

The observation of great mass crimes has revealed a disconcerting reality: among those who committed or allowed them, a majority were not sadists, perverts, or monsters, but ordinary men — family fathers, conscientious employees, people who, under different circumstances, would have led mundane and honest lives.
They did not act out of exceptional cruelty, demonic hatred, but out of conformity, obedience, careerism, cowardice, and a lack of reflection.

The evil they committed was not commensurate with their mediocrity; it is this contrast between the enormity of the crimes and the banality of their authors that struck observers, and which has been termed the banality of evil.
This expression, often misunderstood, does not mean that evil is trivial, nor that crimes are excusable.

It refers to the fact that the perpetrators of great crimes can be ordinary men, that extreme evil can be committed by people who are not monsters, but who, under certain circumstances, influenced by certain mechanisms — obedience to authority, conformity, disempowerment, lack of reflection — become capable of the worst.

Evil does not necessarily require extraordinary wickedness; it can arise from ordinary dispositions and circumstances, from cowardice, conformity, refusal to think, which are within the reach of almost everyone.
This truth is unsettling precisely because it abolishes the reassuring boundary between evil and us.
If great evil were the work of monsters, we would be safe from it, separated from them by a difference in nature.

But if it is committed by ordinary men, under the influence of ordinary mechanisms, then we can no longer believe ourselves to be safe; we must consider that we too, in certain circumstances, could become capable of it.
This thought is unbearable, and that is why we resist it, preferring to believe that we would have remained, we, on the right side.

But this resistance is dangerous, because it is precisely by believing ourselves to be safe that we lower our guard, that we do not monitor within ourselves the dispositions that could lead to the worst.
Recognizing ordinary evil does not excuse criminals, as if their banality justified them; rather, it makes us more vigilant, towards others and towards ourselves.

It invites us to monitor within ourselves the dispositions that make evil possible: blind obedience to authority, conformity that follows the group, the shifting of responsibility onto others, the refusal to think for oneself, the cowardice that does not dare to resist.
It is these ordinary dispositions, more than any exceptional wickedness, that pave the way for the worst.

And to protect ourselves against evil is not to believe ourselves to be of a different species than its authors, but to cultivate within ourselves what resists these mechanisms: the courage to disobey the unjust, the independence that refuses conformity, the responsibility that does not shift, the thought that does not abdicate.
The lesson of ordinary evil is, paradoxically, a lesson in responsibility.

For if evil were the work of monsters, we would have nothing to do but distinguish ourselves from them; but if it can arise in any ordinary person, due to ordinary circumstances and dispositions, then vigilance is our responsibility.

Defending civilization against the barbarism that threatens it is not just about fighting external monsters; it is about monitoring the ordinary dispositions within ourselves and around us that make evil possible, cultivating courage, independence, responsibility, and thought, which alone can resist it.

Ordinary evil teaches us that the line between civilization and barbarism does not run between people, but within each of them — and that it is through each individual, with vigilance and courage, that this line is defended or lost.

alignments.french: Nous aimons croire que le mal, le grand mal, celui des atrocités et des crimes de masse, est l'œuvre de monstres, d'êtres exceptionnellement cruels, radicalement différents de nous.
alignments.english: We like to believe that evil, great evil, the kind associated with atrocities and mass crimes, is the work of monsters, of exceptionally cruel beings, radically different from us.

alignments.french: Cette croyance est rassurante : elle place une frontière nette entre le mal et nous, elle fait des criminels une espèce à part, elle nous préserve de l'inquiétante pensée que nous pourrions, nous aussi, en être capables.
alignments.english: This belief is reassuring: it places a clear boundary between evil and us, it makes criminals a separate species, it protects us from the unsettling thought that we too could be capable of such acts.

alignments.french: Mais cette croyance rassurante est peut-être fausse, et l'une des leçons les plus troublantes de l'histoire récente est que le grand mal est souvent commis non par des monstres, mais par des hommes ordinaires.
alignments.english: But this reassuring belief may be false, and one of the most disturbing lessons of recent history is that great evil is often committed not by monsters, but by ordinary men.

alignments.french: Cette vérité, difficile à admettre, mérite d'être affrontée, car elle éclaire d'un jour cru la fragilité de la civilisation et la nôtre.
alignments.english: This truth, difficult to accept, deserves to be confronted, as it sheds harsh light on the fragility of civilization and our own.

alignments.french: L'observation des grands crimes de masse a révélé une réalité déconcertante : parmi ceux qui les ont commis ou permis, une majorité n'étaient pas des sadiques, des pervers, des monstres, mais des hommes ordinaires — des pères de famille, des employés consciencieux, des gens qui, dans d'autres circonstances, auraient mené des vies banales et honnêtes.
alignments.english: The observation of great mass crimes has revealed a disconcerting reality: among those who committed or allowed them, a majority were not sadists, perverts, or monsters, but ordinary men — family fathers, conscientious employees, people who, under different circumstances, would have led mundane and honest lives.

alignments.french: Ils n'ont pas agi par cruauté exceptionnelle, par haine démoniaque, mais par conformisme, par obéissance, par carriérisme, par lâcheté, par absence de réflexion.
alignments.english: They did not act out of exceptional cruelty, demonic hatred, but out of conformity, obedience, careerism, cowardice, and a lack of reflection.

alignments.french: Le mal qu'ils ont commis n'était pas à la mesure de leur médiocrité ; c'est ce contraste entre l'énormité des crimes et la banalité de leurs auteurs qui a frappé les observateurs, et qu'on a nommé la banalité du mal.
alignments.english: The evil they committed was not commensurate with their mediocrity; it is this contrast between the enormity of the crimes and the banality of their authors that struck observers, and which has been termed the banality of evil.

alignments.french: Cette expression, souvent mal comprise, ne signifie pas que le mal serait anodin, ni que les crimes seraient excusables.
alignments.english: This expression, often misunderstood, does not mean that evil is trivial, nor that crimes are excusable.

alignments.french: Elle désigne le fait que les auteurs de grands crimes peuvent être des hommes ordinaires, que le mal extrême peut être commis par des gens qui ne sont pas des monstres, mais qui, dans certaines circonstances, sous l'effet de certains mécanismes — l'obéissance à l'autorité, le conformisme, la déresponsabilisation, l'absence de réflexion —, deviennent capables du pire.
alignments.english: It refers to the fact that the perpetrators of great crimes can be ordinary men, that extreme evil can be committed by people who are not monsters, but who, under certain circumstances, influenced by certain mechanisms — obedience to authority, conformity, disempowerment, lack of reflection — become capable of the worst.

alignments.french: Le mal ne suppose pas nécessairement une méchanceté extraordinaire ; il peut naître de dispositions et de circonstances ordinaires, de la lâcheté, du conformisme, du refus de penser, qui sont à la portée de presque tous.
alignments.english: Evil does not necessarily require extraordinary wickedness; it can arise from ordinary dispositions and circumstances, from cowardice, conformity, refusal to think, which are within the reach of almost everyone.

sentences: We will die; that is a certainty.
But does something of us remain after our death, and if so, what?

This question, which extends our reflection on finitude, does not concern the survival of the soul here, about which we have seen we cannot decide, but a more modest and certain survival: what we leave in the world, in others, in what outlives us.
For even if we do not believe in life after death, it is undeniable that something of us remains, and it is worth asking what this survival is and what meaning it gives to our mortal existence.
First, we leave a mark on others, on those we have known, loved, and influenced.
Our influence on the beings we have been close to does not die with us; it remains in them, in what we have transmitted, taught, given to them, in the way we have shaped them.
Parents live on in their children, teachers in their students, each in those they have touched.
This survival is not nothing: it is real, it extends our existence beyond our death, in the imprint we have left on other lives.
We live on after our death in memory, in influence, in what we have passed on to those who survive us.
Some of us also leave behind works: creations, achievements, contributions that endure after we are gone.

The artist survives in their work, the thinker in their thoughts, the builder in what they have built; and even the humblest leave something behind — a skill passed on, a contribution to a collective effort, a part of what humanity has accomplished.
This survival in works, when it occurs, can be lasting, far outliving our existence, extending us into the centuries.
But it is not reserved for great creators; everyone, in their own way, contributes to what humanity builds and transmits, thus leaving a part of themselves in the common world.
Finally, we leave the world itself, as marked by our actions.
Each of us, through our lives, contributes to creating the world we leave to those who come after; our actions, our choices, our way of living, shape, however slightly, the world we pass on.
This kind of survival is diffuse, often anonymous, but real: the world after us bears the marks of what we have done, for better or for worse.
We are responsible for what we leave behind, for the world we transmit, for our contribution to what the existence of those who follow us will be.
What value should we assign to this survival in others, in our works, in the world?
It does not fully console us for death, because it is not our personal survival; it is not us who survive, but our mark, our influence, our work.
We will no longer be there to enjoy it, and this survival does not make us immortal.

However, it nonetheless gives meaning to our mortal existence by connecting it to what transcends and prolongs it; it places us in a continuity that exceeds our individual lives, allowing us to participate in something larger and more enduring than ourselves.
Living with the knowledge that we will leave a mark, that we contribute to what will survive, gives mortal life a significance that surpasses its duration.
This thought of what we leave behind has an ethical dimension.
For if we survive in what we leave, then what we leave matters, and we are responsible for it.

Living with the thought of what we will leave — in others, in our works, in the world — means living with the concern of leaving something good, of contributing positively, and not leaving behind ruins or harm.
The awareness of what we leave connects us to the future, makes us responsible for what we pass on, and gives our lives a direction that goes beyond our immediate self-interest.
We do not live only for ourselves, within the limited time of our existence; we also live for what we will leave behind, in the mark we will extend beyond our death.

And perhaps this is a way to give meaning to our mortal condition: not to deny death, but to live in such a way that what we leave behind is worth having been left — that our passage, however brief, adds something good to the world rather than impoverishing it.

sentences: A large French city is studying the possibility of making public transport free for all residents.
The mayor explains that this measure could reduce pollution and help families with a limited budget.
According to him, fewer cars on the streets means cleaner air and less noise.
The project is not new.
Several cities in Europe have already tested free transport, with different results.
In some cities, the number of passengers has increased a lot, which has created very crowded buses and trams during rush hour.
In other cities, the results have been more modest, but residents appreciated paying less each month.
The residents of the city are divided on this idea.
Some find the project excellent.
They think that free transport will encourage more people to leave their cars at home.
A young student explains that she already uses the bus every day to go to university, and that free transport would allow her to save a lot of money each month.
Other residents are more cautious.
They wonder who will pay for this change.
Making public transport free is expensive for the city, and money has to be found somewhere.
A downtown shopkeeper thinks that local taxes will increase to make up for the loss of revenue from bus and metro tickets.
The city council has organized several public meetings to discuss the project with the residents.
During these meetings, transport experts presented figures and studies on cities that have already adopted free transport.
They explained the benefits, such as reducing pollution, but also the challenges, like maintaining vehicles and hiring new drivers.
The mayor promised that a final decision will be made next year, after a long period of study and discussion with the citizens.
A survey will also be organized to know the general opinion of the population before the final vote in the city council.
In the meantime, the city announced a first change: transport will be free on weekends for the next three months, as a trial.
This test will measure the real impact on the number of passengers and on car traffic in the downtown area.
The results of this trial will be presented publicly at the end of the year.
Other French cities are closely following this project.
If the trial is a success, several mayors have already announced that they too would consider making transport free in their own municipalities.
For now, everyone is eagerly awaiting the first results.

sentences: In the northern regions, there was no doubt about it.
Before its disturbances, the compass had never varied in this regard.
Since Cape Saknussemm, we had been drawn directly north for hundreds of leagues.
So, had we returned under Iceland?
Should we be expelled by the crater of Hekla or by those of the seven other volcanic mountains of the island?
Within a radius of 500 leagues to the west, I saw only the poorly known volcanoes of the northwest coast of America beneath this parallel.
In the east, only one existed under the eightieth degree of latitude, the Esk, on the island of Jan Mayen, not far from Spitsbergen!
Certainly, the craters were not lacking, and they were spacious enough to spew out an entire army!
But which one would serve as our exit, that is what I was trying to guess.

sentences: For six months, I haven't taken the car to go to work.
I made this decision after a particularly difficult week in traffic.
Several reasons led me to this change: the price of gas, the stress of traffic jams, and the desire to do something for the environment.
Now, I take the tram, then a bus, to get to the office.
The total journey takes about forty minutes, compared to twenty-five minutes by car before.
At first, this difference in time annoyed me a little.
I was losing fifteen minutes every day.
But I quickly realized that I could use this time differently.
I now read a book during the journey.
In six months, I've read more books than in the previous three years!
I've also saved a lot of money: no more gas, no more parking fees each month.
The only really difficult thing is doing the big shopping without a car.
I now have to do it on foot, with a bag, or ask a friend for help.
Overall, I absolutely do not regret this change.

I sent out more than thirty applications to different companies in my field.
In the first few weeks, I received a lot of negative responses, or often no response at all.
I was starting to seriously worry, because the deadline was approaching quickly.
One morning, when I almost didn't believe it anymore, I received a call from a small company that I had almost forgotten.
They offered me an interview for the following week.
I was both excited and very nervous.
The interview went well.
The manager, Madame Girard, asked me questions about my studies and my plans.
A week later, she called me back to offer me the internship.
I accepted immediately, relieved after so many difficult searches.
The internship lasted three months, and I learned a lot there, much more than I had imagined.
In the end, Madame Girard even offered me a part-time job to continue with them.

sentences: Two years ago, I decided to reduce my wardrobe to thirty pieces, not one more.
I had read an article about what is called a capsule wardrobe, and the idea immediately appealed to me.
At first, the exercise seemed almost impossible.
How could I choose only thirty clothes from the one hundred and fifty I owned?
I started by eliminating what I never wore: gifts that I didn't really like, regretted impulse purchases, and clothes that belonged to another version of myself.
This sorting forced me to ask myself an uncomfortable question: why had I accumulated so many things that I didn't need?
With only thirty pieces, getting dressed in the morning has paradoxically become simpler.
Everything goes with everything, since I chose colors and styles that are consistent with each other.
An unexpected side effect has added to this regained calm: in the morning, choosing an outfit now takes two minutes, not twenty.
Over an entire year, that represents whole hours gained on a decision that, before, exhausted me without me even realizing it.
Some relatives find this approach extreme, almost absurd.
"Don't you get bored wearing the same things all the time?" I am often asked.
In reality, the opposite has happened.
Free from constant choice and accumulation, I now pay more attention to the quality of each piece and less to the quantity.
This experience, which initially seemed like a simple constraint, has become a real way to rethink my relationship with objects in general.

sentences: I check my phone on average, according to an app that counts for me, more than a hundred times a day.
This figure, which I discovered recently, shocked me a bit.
I wasn't aware that I checked my social media so often, almost without thinking, like an automatic gesture.
On one hand, these apps allow me to stay in touch with distant friends, discover interesting ideas, and entertain myself during moments of waiting.
On the other hand, I notice that I sometimes spend twenty minutes scrolling through posts aimlessly, not even remembering afterwards what I saw.
This contradiction interests me: I willingly criticize these apps while continuing to use them very regularly.
I am clearly not the only one in this situation.
I have tried several times to reduce my screen time, with mixed success.
The first few days are always harder than I imagine.

The moments when I check these apps the most almost always correspond to a spike of stress or boredom, as if my phone serves as an automatic reflex in response to discomfort that I prefer to avoid rather than confront directly.
Once this observation is made, at least, I know how to recognize the signal.
I don't think the solution is to completely delete everything; that would probably be excessive for my social and professional life.
But I'm still looking for a satisfying balance between the real usefulness of these tools and the time they consume me despite myself.

sentences: Few public figures inspire such immediate and intense admiration as great athletes.

A sprinter crossing the finish line in a record time, a swimmer breaking a world record by a few hundredths of a second: these moments generate a collective emotion that few other human achievements can provoke so directly.
This admiration deserves to be questioned.

Why do these physical performances, often difficult for the general public to understand in their technical complexity, resonate so much, while significant intellectual or artistic achievements sometimes go almost unnoticed?
A first explanation likely lies in the immediate clarity of athletic performance.

Unlike a complex scientific discovery, which requires explanations to be appreciated, a sports victory is understood instantly: someone has run faster, jumped higher, or endured longer than everyone else.
This clarity of the result facilitates an immediate identification by the public.
A second explanation lies in the bodily dimension of the feat.
The athlete literally embodies, in their own body, the limits we imagine for ourselves.

Seeing them surpass those limits produces a kind of vicarious transcendence, a collective celebration of what the human body can achieve, even for those who do not participate in any sport themselves.
Finally, the fleeting and uncertain nature of competitive sports also plays a role.

Unlike other forms of success, which are built over years without a visible decisive moment, sports performance often unfolds in just a few seconds, on a clearly defined stage, with a winner and losers immediately identified.

This dramatic intensity, concentrated in a very short time, largely explains why sports continue to captivate so many societies around the world, far beyond the mere technical appreciation of the performance itself.

sentences: Certain jurisdictions have recently established a novel legal principle, known as the right to be forgotten, allowing an individual to demand, under certain conditions, the removal of information about themselves that has become outdated or disproportionately harmful in light of the time elapsed since its initial publication.

This principle, as innovative as it is legally delicate to apply, deserves examination regarding what it reveals about the profound transformation that the internet has imposed on the very nature of collective memory.

Before the advent of widespread digital memory, social forgetting operated largely spontaneously, without the need for a specific legal right: yesterday's newspapers faded yellow in archives that few consulted, local rumors died out over time and with the renewal of generations, and an individual's youthful mistakes gradually faded from the collective memory of their surroundings as new events captured the common attention.
This social forgetting, while never perfect or guaranteed, nonetheless offered everyone a real opportunity to start anew, to no longer be indefinitely defined by an old fault or mistake.

The internet has disrupted this old balance by establishing what could be called a quasi-permanent social memory: information published online, no matter how minor it was originally, remains indefinitely accessible, indexed by search engines, and can resurface at any moment, years after its initial interest has faded, permanently associating an individual with a moment in their life that they would have had every chance to see naturally erased from collective memory in the world before.
The right to be forgotten precisely attempts to artificially recreate, through legal means, what spontaneous social forgetting once accomplished without external intervention.
This attempt, while addressing a legitimate concern, faces difficult tensions that are hard to fully resolve.

On one hand, the individual interest in not being indefinitely imprisoned by a past that has passed seems hardly contestable; on the other hand, the freedom of information and the public's right to access a complete and unexpurgated history are equally fundamental principles, the sacrifice of which, even partially, carries its own risks, particularly the risk of allowing public figures to conveniently erase information that is legitimately of public interest.
The practical implementation of this right also encounters considerable difficulties related to the intrinsically transnational nature of the internet.

Information removed in a jurisdiction recognizing the right to be forgotten may very well remain accessible from another country, via another domain name, making the sought erasure largely illusory on a global scale, even if it has been legally obtained at the local level.

This territorial limitation of the right, designed at a time when information still circulated largely according to national borders, struggles to adapt to a digital reality that, by its nature, ignores those same borders.

This tension reveals, more profoundly, that memory has never been a simple individual matter, but has always also been an irreducibly social and collective phenomenon, whose implicit rules — what should be remembered, forgiven, forgotten — were once negotiated informally, through ordinary social practices, and are now imperfectly codified in legal texts that struggle to translate into precise rules what social practice once accomplished with flexibility.

The challenge posed by this new configuration is probably not to definitively settle, once and for all, the conflict between the right to be forgotten and the right to information, two equally legitimate principles that are nonetheless structurally in tension, but to accept that this tension remains permanent, to negotiate on a case-by-case basis, as society learns, not without some trial and error, to live with this digital memory of a permanence for which nothing in all of human history had ever prepared it.

sentences: Hong Kong is just an island, whose possession was assured to England by the Treaty of Nanking after the war of 1842.
In just a few years, Britain's colonial genius had founded an important city there and created a port, Victoria Harbour.
This island is located at the mouth of the Canton River, and only sixty miles separate it from the Portuguese city of Macau, built on the other bank.
Hong Kong had to inevitably surpass Macau in a commercial struggle, and now most of the Chinese transit takes place through the English city.

Docks, hospitals, wharves, warehouses, a Gothic cathedral, a government house, macadamized streets—all of this would make one believe that one of the trading cities from the counties of Kent or Surrey has emerged at this point in China, almost at its antipodes.

Passepartout, with his hands in his pockets, made his way to Victoria Harbour, looking at the palanquins, the sail carts still in favor in the Celestial Empire, and all the crowd of Chinese, Japanese, and Europeans bustling in the streets.
In many ways, it was still Bombay, Calcutta, or Singapore that the worthy boy encountered on his journey.
There is thus a trail of English cities all around the world.

sentences: Listen to me, Fergusson said again.

According to my calculations, we are no more than three hundred miles from the Gulf of Guinea; the desert cannot therefore stretch indefinitely, since the coast is inhabited and recognized up to a certain depth inland.
If necessary, we will head towards that coast, and it is impossible that we won't encounter some oasis, some well where we can replenish our water supply.
But what we lack is the wind, and without it, we are stuck in dead calm in the middle of the air.
--Let's wait with resignation, said the hunter.
But each in turn questioned the empty space in vain during this endless day; nothing appeared that could spark hope.
The last movements of the ground disappeared at sunset, whose horizontal rays stretched out in long lines of fire across this flat expanse.
It was the desert.

The travelers had not covered a distance of fifteen miles, having spent, just like the previous day, one hundred thirty cubic feet of gas to fuel the burner, and two pints of water out of eight had to be sacrificed to quench a burning thirst.
The night passed quietly, too quietly!
The doctor did not sleep.

sentences: For another half hour, our feet treaded on these layers of bones.
We moved forward, driven by a burning curiosity.
What other wonders did this cave hold, what treasures for science?
My gaze was ready for all the surprises, my imagination for all the astonishments.
The shores of the sea had long since disappeared behind the hills of the ossuary.
The reckless professor, caring little about getting lost, was leading me far away.
We advanced silently, bathed in electric waves.
By a phenomenon I cannot explain, and thanks to its complete diffusion at that time, the light illuminated the various surfaces of the objects evenly.
Its focus no longer existed at a specific point in space and it produced no shadow.
One could have believed it was high noon in the middle of summer, in the equatorial regions, under the vertical rays of the sun.

sentences: People admired the wisdom and vigilance of Idomeneus, who had founded such a beautiful kingdom; and everyone concluded that, with peace made with him, the allies would be quite powerful if he joined their league against the Daunians.
It was proposed to Idomeneus that he join; he could not reject such a just proposal, and he promised troops.

But since Mentor was not unaware of everything necessary to make a state flourish, he understood that Idomeneus's forces could not be as great as they appeared; he took him aside and spoke to him like this:
You can see that our efforts have not been in vain.
Salente is safe from the misfortunes that threatened it.
It is now up to you to raise its glory to the heavens and to match the wisdom of Minos, your ancestor, in governing your people.
I continue to speak to you freely, assuming that you want me to and that you detest all flattery.
While these kings praised your magnificence, I was thinking to myself about the recklessness of your conduct.
At the word 'recklessness,' Idomeneus changed his expression, his eyes clouded, he blushed, and he nearly interrupted Mentor to express his resentment.

Mentor said to him in a modest and respectful tone, yet free and bold: 'I see that this word 'recklessness' offends you: anyone else but me would have been wrong to use it; for one must respect kings and be mindful of their sensitivities, even when reprimanding them.'
The truth itself wounds them enough, without adding strong terms; but I believed that you could bear me speaking to you plainly to reveal your fault.

My intention has been to accustom you to hear things named for what they are, and to understand that when others give you advice about your conduct, they will never dare to tell you everything they think.
If you want to avoid being misled, you must always understand more than they will tell you about things that will be disadvantageous to you.
As for me, I am willing to soften my words according to your needs; but it is useful for you that a man without interest and consequence speaks to you in secret a harsh language.
No one else will ever dare to speak to you like this: you will only see the truth partially, and under beautiful coverings.

sentences: We live under observation like no generation before us.
Cameras line the streets, shops, and public transport; our phones record our movements; our activities leave traces everywhere that, when gathered, create a detailed picture of our lives.
This surveillance, widespread and constant, has become so commonplace that we no longer notice it.
However, it's worth pausing to consider what it changes, because being observed is not trivial, and it subtly transforms our way of being.
First, we must measure the scale of the phenomenon.
What distinguishes our time is not the existence of surveillance — those in power have always sought to observe people — but its extent and permanence.
It has never been possible to track the actions and movements of so many people, in such a continuous, detailed manner, at such a low cost.
Surveillance, once limited by its means, has become almost total, extending to areas of existence that until now were beyond any scrutiny.
Being observed changes behavior, even when we have nothing to hide.
Studies confirm this: knowing we are being watched makes us more conforming, more cautious, and less spontaneous.
We monitor ourselves, anticipating the gaze of others and avoiding what might be viewed negatively.
This is not necessarily conscious; it’s a subtle but profound effect.
A society where everyone knows they could be observed is a society where everyone self-censors a bit, where the freedom to be oneself, to diverge, to experiment, is quietly curtailed.
That’s why widespread surveillance poses a problem that goes beyond just privacy.
It touches on freedom itself.
A part of our freedom relies on the existence of spaces removed from observation, where one can be without being seen, think without being judged, and try without fear.
By abolishing these spaces, constant surveillance not only deprives us of intimacy; it shrinks the scope of what we dare to be and do.
An entirely observed world would be a world where boldness, dissent, and simple individuality would become more difficult.
This surveillance has its reasons, one might argue, often good ones: security, prevention, and the proper functioning of services.
That's true, and it shouldn't be rejected outright.
But it is important not to accept it blindly, as if it were an obvious truth without cost.
Each surveillance measure should be weighed: what real benefit is there, and what infringement on freedom does it entail?
Too often, surveillance is adopted for uncertain security gains, without ever measuring what is given up in return.
The question is not "do you have something to hide?", but "what kind of society do we want?".
Living under scrutiny is therefore not a fate we should endure without thinking.
It is a societal choice that affects our freedom as much as our security, and it deserves to be discussed rather than accepted by default.

Preserving spaces without scrutiny, moments without traces, a part of life removed from observation, is not about defending guilty secrets; it is about defending the very conditions of a free existence.

sentences: After optimizing nearly all measurable aspects of our days, part of the professional world now seems to be turning to a final territory to conquer: sleep itself, which is gradually being transformed into a new application of performance logic.

This evolution is concretely manifested through the proliferation of connected devices designed to precisely measure the quality of our nights: the exact duration of different sleep phases, nighttime heart rate, blood oxygen levels, all synthesized into a daily score intended to reflect, with supporting data, the objective quality of our rest.
The initial intention of these tools seems commendable: to help individuals better understand their own sleep cycles, identify potential problems, and adjust their habits accordingly.
For some users, this information has indeed led to concrete and welcome improvements.
However, a paradoxical effect deserves to be noted.

Several sleep specialists are observing the emergence of a phenomenon they call 'orthosomnia': a new anxiety, precisely caused by the obsession with sleeping well according to the criteria measured by these devices, to the point that excessive concern about the nightly score ends up harming natural falling asleep.

Here we touch on a broader paradox of our time: the logic of quantification and constant optimization, initially intended to improve our well-being, risks colonizing even the last spaces of our existence that are still relatively free from this pressure, transforming even rest, which is supposed to liberate us from performance, into a new area of performance in its own right.
Perhaps sleep will remain, despite everything, one of the few domains where the abandonment of control remains, paradoxically, the only truly effective strategy.

sentences: After a week, they had lost all hope.
And Loisel, aged five years, declared:
"We need to find a way to replace this jewel."
The next day, they took the box that had contained it and went to the jeweler whose name was inside.
He consulted his books:
"It wasn't me, madam, who sold this necklace; I only provided the case."
Then they went from jeweler to jeweler, looking for a piece similar to the other, consulting their memories, both sick with grief and anxiety.
They found, in a shop at the Palais-Royal, a string of diamonds that seemed completely similar to the one they were looking for.
It was worth forty thousand francs.
They would be allowed to have it for thirty-six thousand.
So they asked the jeweler not to sell it for three days.
And they made it a condition that it would be taken back for thirty-four thousand francs if the original was found before the end of February.
Loisel had eighteen thousand francs that his father had left him.
He would borrow the rest.
He borrowed, asking for a thousand francs from one, five hundred from another, five louis here, three louis there.
He made promissory notes, took on ruinous commitments, dealt with usurers, and all kinds of lenders.

He jeopardized the rest of his life, risked his signature without even knowing if he could honor it, and, terrified by the anxieties of the future, by the dark misery that was about to fall upon him, by the prospect of all the physical deprivations and all the moral tortures, he went to find the new river, depositing thirty-six thousand francs on the merchant's counter.

sentences: Suddenly, my friend fell silent, got up, then went to take an old paper from his desk, unfolded it, kissed it longingly, and continued.
Here is the will of my beloved mother:
I, the undersigned Anne-Catherine-Geneviève-Mathilde de Croixluce, legitimate wife of Jean-Léopold-Joseph Gontran de Courcils, of sound body and mind, express here my last wishes.
I ask for forgiveness from God first, and then from my dear son René, for the act I am about to commit.
I believe my child is big-hearted enough to understand and forgive me.
I have suffered all my life.
I was married for convenience, then despised, unrecognized, oppressed, and constantly deceived by my husband.
I forgive him, but I owe him nothing.
My older sons did not love me, did not spoil me, and hardly treated me like a mother.
I was for them, during my life, what I was supposed to be; I owe them nothing after my death.
Blood ties do not exist without the constant, sacred affection of each day.
An ungrateful son is less than a stranger; he is guilty, for he has no right to be indifferent to his mother.
I have always trembled before men, before their unjust laws, their inhumane customs, and their infamous prejudices.
Before God, I no longer fear.
Dead, I reject from myself the shameful hypocrisy; I dare to express my thoughts, to confess and sign the secret of my heart.

sentences: She couldn't bear the affront that this wretch inflicted on us, and she asked for permission to travel.
And she left?
The other night.
With Mrs. Danglars?
No, with a relative...
But we won't lose her any less, this dear Eugénie; for I doubt that with the character I know her to have, she will ever agree to return to France!
What do you want, my dear baron, said Monte-Cristo, family troubles, troubles that would be crushing for a poor devil whose child is his whole fortune, but bearable for a millionaire.

Philosophers may say what they like, practical men will always contradict them on this: money consoles for many things; and you, you must be consoled more quickly than anyone else, if you accept the virtue of this sovereign balm: you, the king of finance, the intersection point of all powers.
Danglars cast a sidelong glance at the count to see if he was joking or speaking seriously.
"Yes," he said, "the fact is that if fortune consoles, I must be consoled: I am rich.
So rich, my dear baron, that your fortune resembles the Pyramids; even if one wanted to demolish them, one wouldn't dare; if one dared, one couldn't."
Danglars smiled at this confident simplicity of the count.
That reminds me, he said, that when you entered, I was in the process of making five small notes; I had already signed two; would you allow me to make the other three?
--Go ahead, my dear baron, go ahead.
There was a moment of silence, during which the banker’s pen could be heard scratching, while Monte-Cristo looked at the gilded moldings on the ceiling.
"Notes from Spain, said Monte-Cristo, notes from Haiti, notes from Naples?
--No, said Danglars, laughing his self-satisfied laugh, bearer notes, notes on the Bank of France.
Here, he added, Mr. Count, you who are the emperor of finance, just as I am the king, have you seen many pieces of paper of this size worth a million each?"
Monte-Cristo took in his hand, as if to weigh them, the five pieces of paper that Danglars proudly presented to him, and read:
"May it please Mr. Regent of the Bank to pay to my order, and from the funds deposited by me, the sum of one million, value in account.

sentences: And Mercédès raised her beautiful eyes to the sky with such infinite gratitude that the count believed he saw two tears trembling there.
Mr. de Morcerf approached her.
"Madam," he said, "I have already apologized to Mr. the Count for having to leave him, and I ask you to renew my apologies to him.
The meeting starts at two o'clock, it is three now, and I must speak.
--Go on, sir, I will try to make our host forget your absence," said the countess with the same tone of sensitivity.
"Mr. Count," she continued, turning to Monte-Cristo, "will you do us the honor of spending the rest of the day with us?
--Thank you, madam, and believe me, you see me more grateful than ever for your offer; but I arrived this morning at your door from my traveling carriage.
How I am settled in Paris, I do not know; where I am, I can barely tell.
It is a slight worry, I know, but still appreciable.
--We will have this pleasure another time, at least you promise us that?" asked the countess.
Monte-Cristo bowed without answering, but the gesture could be taken as an assent.
"Then, I won't keep you, sir," said the countess, "for I do not want my gratitude to become either an indiscretion or an imposition.

My dear count, said Albert, if you don't mind, I will try to return to Paris your gracious politeness from Rome, and put my carriage at your disposal until you have had time to arrange your own vehicles.

Thank you a thousand times for your kindness, viscount, said Monte-Cristo, but I assume that Mr. Bertuccio has properly used the four and a half hours that I just left him, and that I will find a carriage waiting for me at the door.

Albert was used to these manners from the count: he knew that he was, like Nero, in search of the impossible, and he was no longer surprised by anything; however, he wanted to judge for himself how his orders had been executed, so he accompanied him to the hotel door.

Monte-Cristo was not mistaken: as soon as he appeared in the antechamber of the count of Morcerf, a footman, the same one who had come in Rome to bring the count's card to the two young men and announce his visit, rushed out of the peristyle, so that upon arriving at the steps, the illustrious traveler indeed found his carriage waiting for him.

sentences: Five minutes after the telegram arrived at the ministry, Debray had the horses put to his carriage and ran to Danglars' house.
"Does your husband have any coupons from the Spanish loan?" he asked the baroness.
"I certainly believe so! He has six million worth."
"Let him sell them at any price."
"Why is that?"
"Because Don Carlos has escaped from Bourges and returned to Spain."
"How do you know that?"
"Of course," said Debray, shrugging his shoulders, "just like I know the news."
The baroness didn't need to be told twice: she ran to her husband, who in turn ran to his stockbroker and ordered him to sell at any cost.
When it was seen that Mr. Danglars was selling, the Spanish stocks immediately dropped.
Danglars lost five hundred thousand francs on it, but he got rid of all his coupons.

sentences: Mrs. Paulina Barnett was looking at the map in silence!

sentences: I need to collect my thoughts, to refresh my memories, to control my own statements.
The last words of the Canadian had caused a sudden shift in my mind.
I quickly climbed to the top of the being or object that was half-submerged and served as our refuge.
I tested it with my foot.
It was obviously a hard, impenetrable body, and not that soft substance that makes up the mass of large marine mammals.
But this hard body could be a bony shell, similar to those of prehistoric animals, and I would have to classify the monster among amphibious reptiles, such as turtles or alligators.
Well! No!
The dark back that supported me was smooth, polished, and not interlocked.
It produced a metallic sound upon impact, and, as incredible as it was, it seemed that, I say, it was made of bolted plates.
There was no doubt about it!

The animal, the monster, the natural phenomenon that had intrigued the entire scientific world, disrupted and misled the imagination of sailors from both hemispheres, it must be acknowledged, was an even more astonishing phenomenon, a phenomenon of human hands.
The discovery of the existence of the most fabulous, the most mythical being, would not have surprised my reason to the same degree.
That what is extraordinary comes from the Creator is quite simple.

sentences: But how did they manage to transport these two fish to Paris?

sentences: Well then, Master Pastrini, Franz replied, now that my companion is calm and you have been able to appreciate my peaceful intentions, let's see who Lord Luigi Vampa is.
Is he a shepherd or a patrician? Is he young or old? Is he short or tall?
Describe him to us, so that if we happen to meet him in the world, like Jean Sbogar or Lara, we can at least recognize him.

--You couldn't have chosen better than to ask me, Your Excellency, for accurate details, as I have known Luigi Vampa since he was a child; and one day, when I myself fell into his hands while traveling from Ferentino to Alatri, he fortunately remembered our old acquaintance; he let me go, not only without demanding a ransom, but even after giving me a very fine watch and telling me his story.
--Let's see the watch," said Albert.
Master Pastrini pulled out a magnificent Breguet from his pocket, bearing the name of its maker, the Paris stamp, and a count's crown.
"Here it is," he said.
--Wow! exclaimed Albert, I compliment you on that; I have a similar one—he took his watch out of his waistcoat pocket—and it cost me three thousand francs.
--Let's hear the story, Franz said in turn, pulling up a chair and signaling for Master Pastrini to sit down.
--Do Your Excellencies permit? asked the host.
--Indeed! said Albert, you are not a preacher, my dear, to speak while standing."
The innkeeper sat down after respectfully bowing to each of his future listeners, which was meant to indicate that he was ready to provide them with the information they requested about Luigi Vampa.

sentences: Edmond heard the noise of the bed on which the corpse was being moved; he heard the governor's voice, who ordered that water be thrown in the prisoner's face, and seeing that, despite this immersion, the prisoner did not come back to life, sent for the doctor.
The governor left; and a few words of compassion reached Dantès's ears, mixed with mocking laughter.
"Come on, come on, one of them said, the fool has gone to join his treasures, safe travels!
--He won't have, with all his millions, enough to pay for his shroud, said the other.
--Oh! replied a third voice, the shrouds from the Château d'If are not expensive.
--Perhaps, said one of the first speakers, since he is a man of the Church, some expenses will be made on his behalf.
--Then he will receive the honors of the sacristy."
Edmond was listening, not missing a word, but he didn't understand much of all this.
Soon the voices faded away, and it seemed to him that the attendants were leaving the room.
However, he did not dare to go back in: they might have left some keyholder to guard the dead.
He remained silent, motionless, and holding his breath.
After about an hour, the silence was stirred by a faint noise that grew louder.
It was the governor returning, followed by the doctor and several officers.
There was a moment of silence: it was clear that the doctor was approaching the bed and examining the corpse.
Soon the questions began.
The doctor analyzed the illness that the prisoner had succumbed to and declared that he was dead.
Questions and answers were exchanged with a nonchalance that outraged Dantès; it seemed to him that everyone should feel for the poor abbé a part of the affection he had for him.

sentences: The old baron of Ravots had been the king of hunters in his province for forty years.
But for the past five or six years, paralysis in his legs had kept him stuck in his chair, and he could only shoot pigeons from the window of his living room or from the top of his grand porch.
The rest of the time he read.
He was a pleasant businessman who still had much of the literary spirit of the last century.
He loved stories, particularly naughty little tales, as well as true stories that happened around him.
As soon as a friend entered his home, he would ask:
--So, what's new?
And he knew how to question like an investigating judge.
On sunny days, he would roll his large chair, which resembled a bed, in front of the door.

A servant, behind his back, held the guns, loaded them, and passed them to his master; another servant, hidden in a bush, would occasionally release a pigeon at irregular intervals so that the baron wouldn't be warned and would stay alert.
And from morning till night, he shot at the fast birds, lamenting when he was caught off guard, and laughing to tears when the creature fell straight down or did some unexpected and funny tumble.
He would then turn to the boy who was loading the guns and would ask, gasping with joy:
There he is, that one, Joseph!
Did you see how he came down?
And Joseph would invariably reply:
Oh! the baron never misses them.
In the autumn, during the hunting season, he would invite his friends, as in the old days, and he loved to hear the gunshots in the distance.
He counted them, happy when they came in quick succession.
And in the evening, he demanded a faithful account of the day from each of them.

sentences: As long as I understand your treachery, sir, and manage to make you understand that I want to take my revenge, I will always be reasonable enough, said Albert furiously.
Sir, I do not understand you at all, replied Monte-Cristo, and even if I did understand you, you would still be speaking too loudly.
I am at home here, sir, and only I have the right to raise my voice above the others.
Get out, sir!
And Monte-Cristo pointed to the door for Albert with an admirable gesture of command.
"Ah! I will certainly make you leave your own home!" Albert replied, crumpling his glove in his convulsive hands, which the count was keeping an eye on.

"Well, well!" said Monte-Cristo phlegmatically; "you are looking for a quarrel, sir; I see that; but here’s some advice, viscount, and remember it well: it is a bad habit to make noise when provoking someone.
Noise does not suit everyone, Monsieur de Morcerf."
At that name, a murmur of astonishment passed like a shiver among the spectators of this scene.
Since the day before, the name Morcerf had been on everyone's lips.

Albert, better than anyone else, and the first of all, understood the allusion, and made a gesture to throw his glove in the count's face; but Morrel seized his wrist, while Beauchamp and Château-Renaud, fearing that the scene might go beyond mere provocation, held him back from behind.
But Monte-Cristo, without getting up, leaning back in his chair, simply extended his hand and seized the damp, crushed glove between the young man's clenched fingers:
Sir, he said with a terrible accent, I consider your glove thrown, and I will send it to you rolled around a bullet.
Now, get out of my house, or I will call my servants and have you thrown out the door.

sentences: The servant of our inn was at most eighteen years old, with bright blue eyes, a pale blue pierced by the two small black dots of her pupils; and her short, tightly packed teeth, which she constantly showed while laughing, seemed made for crushing granite.
She didn't know a word of French, speaking only Breton, like most of her compatriots.
However, my friend wasn't getting any better, and although no illness had been diagnosed, the doctor forbade him from leaving yet, ordering complete rest.
So I spent my days near him, and the little maid kept coming in, bringing either my dinner or some herbal tea.
I teased her a bit, which seemed to amuse her, but we didn't talk, of course, since we couldn't understand each other.
One night, as I had stayed very late by the sick man's side, I crossed paths, on my way back to my room, with the little girl who was returning to hers.

It was right in front of my open door; then, suddenly, without thinking about what I was doing, more as a joke than anything else, I grabbed her around the waist, and before she could recover from her shock, I had thrown her in and locked her in my room.
She looked at me, terrified, frantic, horrified, not daring to scream for fear of causing a scandal, of being thrown out first by her masters, and perhaps later by her father.
I had done this while laughing; but as soon as she was in my room, the desire to possess her overwhelmed me.
It was a long and silent struggle, a struggle hand-to-hand, like athletes, with our arms stretched, tense, twisted, breathless, our skin wet with sweat.

Oh! she fought back valiantly; and sometimes we bumped into a piece of furniture, a wall, a chair; then, still entangled, we remained motionless for several seconds, fearing that the noise might have awakened someone; then we would resume our fierce battle, with me attacking and her resisting.

sentences: In this vault, the body of poor Renée had already been laid to rest, which her father and mother were coming to join after ten years of separation.

Paris, always curious and always moved by funeral pomp, witnessed in religious silence the splendid procession that accompanied to their final resting place two of the names from this old aristocracy, the most famous for their traditional spirit, for the security of commerce, and for their stubborn dedication to principles.
In the same funeral carriage, Beauchamp, Albert, and Château-Renaud were discussing this almost sudden death.

"I saw Madame de Saint-Méran last year in Marseille," Château-Renaud said, "I was returning from Algeria; she was a woman destined to live a hundred years, thanks to her perfect health, her ever-present mind, and her always prodigious activity.
How old was she?
--Sixty-six, Albert replied, at least according to what Franz assured me.
But it wasn't age that killed her; it was the grief she felt from the marquis's death; apparently, since that death, which had shaken her violently, she hasn't fully regained her sanity.
--But what did she die of? Beauchamp asked.
--Of a cerebral congestion, it seems, or a sudden apoplexy.
Isn't that the same thing?
--Pretty much.
--Apoplexy? said Beauchamp, it's hard to believe.

Mme de Saint-Méran, whom I have seen once or twice in my life, was small, slender in build, and of a constitution much more nervous than sanguine; apoplexies caused by grief are rare in a body with a constitution like that of Mme de Saint-Méran.

sentences: I believed, however, the traveler replied, that since it absorbed the old Northwest Company, the Hudson's Bay Company found itself without competitors on the American continent.
Sir, replied Jasper Hobson, if there is no longer any significant association engaged in the fur trade outside of ours, there are still perfectly independent private associations.
In general, these are American companies that have retained agents or descendants of French agents in their service.
So these agents were held in high regard? asked Mrs. Paulina Barnett.
Certainly, madam, and rightly so.
During the ninety-four years of French supremacy in Canada, these French agents consistently proved superior to ours.

sentences: While I was in this uncertainty, suddenly I hear a voice more than human: I see Hercules in a shining cloud; he was surrounded by rays of glory.
I easily recognized his somewhat rugged features, his robust body, and his simple manners; but he had a height and majesty that had never seemed so great in him when he was taming monsters.
He said to me: You hear, you see Hercules.
I have left high Olympus to announce to you the orders of Jupiter.
You know by what labors I have gained immortality: you must go with the son of Achilles to follow in my footsteps on the path to glory.
You will heal; you will pierce Paris, the source of so many evils, with my arrows.
After the fall of Troy, you will send rich spoils to your father Pæon on Mount Œta; these spoils will be placed on my tomb as a monument to the victory due to my arrows.
And you, O son of Achilles! I declare to you that you cannot conquer without Philoctetes, nor Philoctetes without you.
So go like two lions who seek their prey together.
I will see Asclepius in Troy to heal Philoctetes.
Above all, O Greeks, love and observe religion: the rest dies; it never dies.
After hearing these words, I exclaimed: O happy day, sweet light, you finally show yourself after so many years!
I obey you; I leave after bidding farewell to this place.
Farewell, dear cave.
Farewell, nymphs of these damp meadows.
I will no longer hear the muffled sound of the waves of this sea.
Farewell, shore where I have so often suffered the insults of the air.
Farewell, promontory where Echo repeated my groans so many times.
Farewell, sweet fountains that were so bitter to me.
Farewell, O land of Lemnos; let me depart happily, since I am going where the will of the gods and my friends calls me!
So we set off: we arrived at the siege of Troy.
Machaon and Podalyre, through the divine knowledge of their father Esculape, healed me, or at least brought me to the state you see me in now.
I no longer suffer; I have regained all my strength: but I am a bit lame.
I brought down Paris like a timid fawn that a hunter pierces with his arrows.
Soon Ilion was reduced to ashes; you know the rest.

I still had some sort of aversion for the wise Ulysses, due to the memory of my sufferings; and his virtue could not soothe this resentment: but the sight of a son who resembles him, and whom I cannot help but love, softened my heart for the father himself.

In the warm season, the widened bank revealed the garden walls down to their base, which had a few steps leading down to the river.
It flowed silently, swift and cold to the eye; tall, slender grasses bent together according to the current that pushed them, and, like abandoned green hair, spread out in its clarity.
Sometimes, at the tip of the reeds or on the leaf of the water lilies, an insect with fine legs walked or landed.

The sun pierced through a ray the small blue globules of the waves that followed one another as they broke; the old, branchless willows mirrored their gray bark in the water; the meadow beyond seemed empty; it was dinner time on the farms, and the young woman and her companion heard only the rhythm of their footsteps on the path's earth, the words they exchanged, and the rustling of Emma's dress that whispered all around her.
