The following day rose sad and cloudy.

The undertakers had carried out their funeral duties during the night, and had sewn the body laid on the bed into the shroud that grimly drapes the deceased, lending them, in a way that speaks to the equality in death, a final testament to the luxury they loved in life.
This shroud was nothing other than a piece of magnificent batiste that the young girl had bought fifteen days earlier.
In the evening, men called for this purpose had moved Noirtier from Valentine's room to his own, and, against all expectations, the old man had shown no reluctance to leave his child's body.
Abbé Busoni had kept watch until dawn, and at daybreak, he had withdrawn to his home without calling anyone.
Around eight in the morning, d'Avrigny returned; he had met Villefort who was passing by Noirtier's, and he accompanied him to find out how the old man had spent the night.
They found him in the large armchair that served as his bed, resting in a gentle and almost smiling sleep.
Both of them stopped, astonished, on the threshold.

"Look," said d'Avrigny to Villefort, who was watching his father sleep; "look, nature knows how to soothe the deepest pains; certainly, one cannot say that Mr. Noirtier did not love his granddaughter; yet he sleeps.
--Yes, and you are right," Villefort replied in surprise; "he sleeps, and it is quite strange, for the slightest annoyance keeps him awake for entire nights.
--The pain has overwhelmed him," d'Avrigny replied.
And both of them returned thoughtfully to the prosecutor's office.

"Look, I haven't slept," Villefort said, pointing to his untouched bed; "pain doesn't overwhelm me, I've not gone to bed for two nights; but in exchange, look at my desk; have I written, my God! during these two days and two nights!... have I gone through this file, have I annotated this indictment of the assassin Benedetto!...
"Oh work, work! my passion, my joy, my rage, it's up to you to conquer all my pains!"
And he grasped d'Avrigny's hand convulsively.
"Do you need me?" the doctor asked.
"No," Villefort said; "just come back at eleven, please; it's at noon that... the departure..."
"My God! my poor child! my poor child!"

sentences: This year, I have a project: a small vegetable garden behind the house.
My neighbor, Mrs. Petit, tells me: "It's easy!
You need sunlight, water, and patience."
In April, I prepare the soil.
It's a workout!
Then I plant tomatoes, lettuce, carrots, and basil.
Every day, I water my garden.
I wait.
One week, nothing.
Two weeks.
And one morning: small green leaves!
I am proud.
But the snails love my salad.
Every morning, I find holes in the leaves.
Madame Petit tells me, "Put sand around the salad."
It works!
In June, the tomatoes are green.
In July, they turn red.
I eat the first red tomato directly in the garden.
It is sweet.
Tonight, I am making a big salad with my vegetables.
My whole family eats my work.
"It's delicious!" says my wife.
Madame Petit is right.
Sun, water, patience, and a little love.
Before getting a job, you often have to go through a stressful step: the job interview.
I had my first interview two years ago, and I still remember my hands shaking.
To apply, I had sent my resume and a cover letter.
A few days later, the company called me to offer a meeting.
I was happy, but also very worried.
How should I present myself?
What should I say?
What should I wear?
A friend who had already hired people gave me some advice.
The boss isn't looking for someone perfect, he explained to me.
He wants to know if you are motivated, honest, and if you will work well with your future colleagues.
On the day of the interview, I arrived early.
The recruiter asked me a lot of questions: about my studies, about my skills, about my strengths and weaknesses.
The most difficult one was: 'Why do you want this position?'
I answered honestly, in my own words.
At the end, she asked me if I had any questions.
I had prepared two; this shows that you are really interested in the job.
A week later, good news: I got hired!
Since then, I've had other interviews, and I'm still a bit nervous.
But I understood that it's not an exam: it's simply a conversation between two people who are trying to get to know each other.

sentences: On Tuesday, at the supermarket, my bank card didn't work.
I had a full cart and there were four people behind me.
The cashier tried twice.
"Card declined," said the machine.
I was very embarrassed.
Fortunately, I had some cash in my bag.
I was able to pay.
But I didn't understand why.
I was sure I had money in my account.
In the evening, I checked online.
My account was fine.
So what was the problem?
I called my bank.
I waited fifteen minutes with horrible music.
Then a voice said, "All our lines are busy.
Please call back later."
And then it hung up!
I was annoyed.
The next morning, I went directly to the agency.
I waited ten minutes, then an advisor saw me.
I explained the problem to him.
He looked at his computer for a minute.
Ah, I see.
Your card expired at the end of last month.
We sent you a new card three weeks ago.
A new card?
I hadn't received anything.
Then I thought and I understood.
There was an envelope from the bank on my desk at home.
I had never opened it.
The advisor smiled.
It happens often, you know.
In the evening, I opened the envelope.
My new card was inside.
Last summer, we had a heatwave.
It was over forty degrees for six days.
I had never experienced that in my region.
Normally, in July, it is twenty-eight or thirty degrees.
In the first few days, everyone talked about it with a smile: "What heat!"
But after three days, no one was smiling anymore.
The hardest part was at night.
The temperature didn't go below twenty-eight degrees.
I slept very poorly.
I opened the windows, but the air was hot too.
The city changed completely.
During the day, the streets were empty.
People closed the shutters as early as nine in the morning to keep a bit of coolness.
My neighbor, who is eighty-two years old, no longer went out.
My mother called her twice a day to check that she was drinking water.
Elderly people are the most at risk during a heatwave.
The town hall opened an air-conditioned room.
Many people spent the afternoon there.
Starting at nine in the evening, everyone went out at the same time.
The streets filled up.
It was strange: life began at night.
On the seventh day, a storm arrived.
The temperature dropped by twelve degrees in one hour.
People went out in the rain.
Some were applauding.

sentences: I'm too old to learn that.
This phrase is one of the most common, and one of the least accurate.
The adult brain retains a capacity for learning throughout life.
This phenomenon has a name, brain plasticity, and it is well established: connections reorganize based on what we practice, at thirty as well as at seventy.
That doesn't mean there is no difference.
Some things are indeed easier when young, especially acquiring a perfect accent in a foreign language.

But adults have real and underestimated advantages: they understand structures, make connections with what they already know, choose their methods, and know why they are learning — a chosen motivation is better than an imposed one.
What mainly changes are the conditions.
An adult has less time, more fatigue, and much more fear of ridicule.
This fear is probably the main obstacle, well before age.
Research on learning provides some solid principles that apply at any age.
Spaced repetition beats massed repetition: three times twenty minutes in the week is better than one hour on Sunday.
Testing yourself is more effective than rereading.
Trying to remember, even if you don't succeed, anchors you more than just going over the text.
Finally, moderate difficulty is useful: what is too easy doesn't teach anything.
So the question is not whether you can still learn.
It is whether you are willing to be bad for a few weeks.

sentences: What is the purpose of history?
We cannot change the past.
This objection seems solid.
However, it is based on a false idea of what history is.
Studying history is not about memorizing dates.
It is about learning a way of reasoning, and this way applies well beyond the past.
The historian works with sources: documents, testimonies, objects.
Each source has an author, an intention, and limitations.
The same event is told differently depending on who writes it.
The job consists precisely of confronting these narratives, identifying the silences, and distinguishing a fact from an opinion.
And that's exactly what we need to do every day when faced with information.
Who is speaking?
In whose interest?
What are they not saying?
The historical method is, in fact, an education in critical thinking.
History also teaches complexity.
Events have multiple causes; the actors are neither entirely good nor entirely bad; a decision that seems obvious today was not so at the time, given the information available then.
This caution is valuable in an era that loves simple explanations.
It also makes us more humble.
By seeing how many societies believed they held a definitive truth, we put our own certainties into perspective.
There is a commonly quoted phrase: "Those who do not know history are condemned to repeat it."
It is partly true, but a bit naive: history never repeats itself exactly.
Its usefulness is more subtle.
It does not predict the future.
It teaches you not to believe the first story you hear.

sentences: There have always been poor people, and there always will be.
This phrase, often spoken with an air of wisdom, expresses a fatalism that treats poverty as an inevitable aspect of the human condition, a natural fact against which it would be futile to fight.
This fatalism is convenient: it relieves one from acting, it soothes the conscience, and it makes inaction a form of clarity.
But it is based on a confusion and an error that must be brought to light, for poverty is not the fatality that it is claimed to be.
First, we must distinguish between two concepts that fatalism confuses: absolute poverty and relative poverty.
Absolute poverty is the lack of essential necessities — food, shelter, healthcare, survival.
Relative poverty is having much less than others in a given society, without necessarily lacking the essentials.

These two realities are quite different, and fatalism mixes them to seem more justified: "we will never eliminate all poverty" is plausible if it refers to relative poverty, which always allows for possible disparities; but it is false if it refers to absolute poverty, that of lacking essentials, which is not inevitable.
For absolute poverty, far from being a fatality, has significantly decreased in recent history, and there is nothing to prevent us from thinking that it could be eradicated.
Today, we produce enough to feed, house, and care for all of humanity; the persistence of misery is not due to a shortage of resources, but to their distribution.
That human beings lack essentials in a world that produces more than enough to meet everyone's needs is not a natural fatality, but the result of organization, choices, and power dynamics.
Absolute misery is not inscribed in the nature of things; it is a problem we could solve, and that we tolerate.
Fatalism about poverty thus serves a purpose: it transforms a solvable problem into an insurmountable fate, thereby legitimizing inaction.
By presenting poverty as inevitable, it discourages any effort to combat it, makes resignation appear as wisdom, and absolves a society that could do much more.

That is why this fatalism, under its guise of realism, is actually an ideology: it serves the interests of those who do not want to change the existing order, persuading everyone that there is nothing to be done.
"There's nothing we can do" is the best ally of "I don't want to do anything."
Recognizing that absolute poverty is not a fatality does not mean claiming that it would be easy to eradicate it, nor ignoring the complexity of the obstacles.

The distribution of resources faces powerful interests, real difficulties, and perverse effects that must be anticipated; combating poverty is not simple, and naive solutions can worsen the ills they claim to heal.
But difficulty is not the same as impossibility, and recognizing that something is difficult is very different from declaring it fatal.
We can debate ways to reduce poverty; we cannot take refuge in the idea that it is inevitable in order to avoid trying.
As for relative poverty and wealth disparities, the question is different and more complex, as some inequality may be inevitable, or even, within certain limits, acceptable.
But even there, the extent of the disparities is not fatal: they have varied greatly over time and across societies, which proves that they depend on choices and not on an immutable nature.
The persistence of poverty, whether absolute or relative, is never a simple fatality; it is always, in part, the result of what we do and do not do.
The fatalism that naturalizes it is the first thing to combat, because as long as we consider a problem to be inevitable, we do not even seek to heal it.

sentences: He belonged to the great surgical school that emerged from Bichat's apron, to that now-disappeared generation of philosopher practitioners who, cherishing their art with a fanatical love, practiced it with exaltation and sagacity!

Everything trembled in his hospital when he got angry, and his students revered him so much that they tried, as soon as they were established, to imitate him as closely as possible; so much so that one could find them, in the surrounding towns, wearing his long merino dressing gown and his large black coat, the unbuttoned lapels covering his fleshy hands—very beautiful hands that never wore gloves, as if to be quicker to plunge into misery.

Disdainful of crosses, titles, and academies, hospitable, liberal, paternal with the poor, and practicing virtue without believing in it, he would have almost passed for a saint if the sharpness of his mind hadn't made him feared like a demon.

His gaze, sharper than his scalpels, pierced straight into the soul and dismantled every lie through allegations and modesties.—And he walked like this, full of that benevolent majesty that comes from the awareness of great talent, fortune, and forty years of a laborious and irreproachable existence.
He frowned as soon as he entered, upon seeing Emma's cadaverous face, lying on her back, her mouth open.
Then, while pretending to listen to Canivet, he rubbed his index finger under his nose and repeated, "It's fine, it's fine."
But he made a slow gesture with his shoulders.
Bovary observed him: they looked at each other; and this man, so accustomed to the sight of suffering, could not hold back a tear that fell onto his jabot.
He wanted to take Canivet into the next room, and Charles followed him.
"She is very ill, isn't she?"
"If only we could apply some mustard plasters! I don't know what! Find something, you who have saved so many!"
Charles was wrapping his arms around her body, and he was looking at her in a way that was terrified, pleading, half-fainting against his chest.
Come now! My poor boy, be brave! There's nothing more to be done.--And Doctor Larivière turned away.
Are you leaving?
I will be back.
He went out as if to give an order to the postilion, with Monsieur Canivet, who also didn't care to see Emma die in his hands.
